A: Coronal weight-bearing CT in article titled Acquired Pes Planovalgus with caption misalignment of subtalar joint and in-text increased valgus tilt of posterior facet, visible valgus angulation. B: Coronal WBCT with captioned sinus tarsi impingement and medial facet subluxation in acquired pes planovalgus article, manifestation of hindfoot valgus collapsing deformity. C: Coronal WBCT with captioned subfibular impingement and posterior facet subluxation in acquired pes planovalgus article, valgus-related hindfoot deformity. D: Sagittal weight-bearing CT with captioned instability with plantar opening of tarsometatarsal joint and visual flat sagittal arch in acquired pes planovalgus article.

panels.figure_caption: Coronal weight-bearing computed tomography scan demonstrating: ( A ) the misalignment of the subtalar joint; ( B ) sinus tarsi impingement and medial facet subluxation; and ( C ) subfibular impingement and posterior facet subluxation. ( D ) Sagittal scan demonstrating instability with the plantar opening of the tarsometatarsal joint.
in_text_mentions: If available, a hindfoot alignment view is strongly recommended, as is weight-bearing computed tomography (WCT). A WBCT scan from patients with the deformity reveals important findings, such as sinus tarsi impingement, subfibular impingement, increased valgus tilt of the posterior facet of the subtalar joint, and subluxation of the subtalar joint at the posterior and middle facets or both 10 11 ( Fig. 1 ).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Patient MRI panel from an AAFD imaging review explicitly captioned as showing posterior tibial tendon pathology, the key static/dynamic structure in adult acquired flatfoot; arrow annotation present. b: Patient axial T2 MRI panel captioned as showing the superomedial fibers of the spring ligament, whose injury leads to plano-valgus deformity in adult acquired flatfoot; no exact vocabulary finding key exists for spring ligament injury, so it is proposed. Article title establishes the AAFD context.
panels.attribution_text: Polichetti et al. Adult Acquired Flatfoot Deformity: A Narrative Review about Imaging Findings.. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2023. doi:10.3390/diagnostics13020225. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 10.
panels.figure_caption: Magnetic Resonance Imaging. (a) Coronal T1: soft tissue involvement of the posterior tibial tendon, (b) Axial T2: superomedial fibers of the spring ligament (white arrow).
in_text_mentions: MRI is the preferred modality for assessment of the PTT (Figure 10a) and it has a good accuracy in showing tendon abnormalities, with a sensitivity of up to 95% and a specificity of 100% in the detection of the rupture of the PTT [30]. The PTT can be affected by degenerative tendinosis, tenosynovitis, and a partial or complete tear. PTT tendinosis can be diagnosed with increased signal intensity in the tendon with preservation of the normal shape; tenosynovitis (isolated) is documented if there is a high fluid signal intensity surrounding 50% or more of the PTT circumference with normal size,

The spring ligament (Figure 10b), also known as the plantar calcaneo-navicular ligament, is considered the primary static stabilizer of the medial arch and is second in importance only to the PTT [7]. The superomedial component of the spring ligament complex is the largest and most important part and constitutes a structure that supports the talar head and talonavicular joint and separates the PTT from the talus bone.
